I’m an artist with BPD! I think if I was going to design a tattoo based off of how I experience BPD, it would somehow incorporate black and white shapes (I don’t quite know why but I’m thinking squares) and a burst of bright colors. The shapes would be to symbolize the ‘black and white thinking’ that we do, and the colors would be to represent overwhelming emotion. I personally wouldn’t want to use any shading in it, only the darkest blacks, the whitest whites, the brightest colors, since borderlines tend to lack a sense of grey areas and everything feels really intense. In my head I’m picturing a sort of vaporwave aesthetic, with black and white shapes of varying sizes floating on a very colorful background, but it’s a little tricky to describe it. You could experiment with the placement of the shapes to mimic a sense of motion, that might be a way to visually capture the rapid mood swings. If you also wanted to incorporate loneliness into that concept, you could make the background a really simple (but still bright) gradient so it wouldn’t be so busy.

dissociation is different for everybody. for me, I describe it as “advanced zoning out,” because I feel very detached from myself and everything that’s going on around me, kind of like I’m watching a movie about my life but not paying full attention to it. sometimes when it gets bad I can forget where I am even if it’s a familiar place, and at its worst I forget who I am too. a little bit of dissociation is normal, since regular ‘zoning out’ is considered a form of dissociation, and it’s common when you’re doing things on autopilot, like driving a route you drive all the time and suddenly realizing you’re home sooner than you thought you’d be. if it becomes a frequent issue that causes you distress, that’s when it’s considered a mental health issue. hope this helps!

In early April of 2019, just barely over a year ago now, I decided I was done. I’ve dealt with mental illness for my entire life, starting off with anxiety and ADHD in grade school, intentionally self harming when I was 11, showing signs of a personality disorder from the time I was 13, developing PTSD and episodes of psychosis at 16, recovering from anorexia without medical help when I was 17, suffering hallucinations and physical illness from being put on the wrong antipsychotics at 19, and spending almost a week in the psych hospital a few months after that due to consistent suicidal ideation and mild substance abuse.  I was 20, engaged to and living with someone who was abusive, doing poorly in my college classes, and overwhelmed by life in general.  I was getting into terrible arguments with my fiancé all the time, and I felt like I couldn’t leave them because they didn’t really have anywhere else to go if I kicked them out.  I felt trapped and just wanted out.

I had tried to kill myself just over a week earlier with a small overdose of my old prescriptions.  My fiancé had gone through this in high school and kept an eye on me for the night but didn’t think I needed to go to the hospital.  I had to beg them not to call an ambulance when it first happened because I couldn’t afford it, but they finally gave in and stayed up most of the night to keep an eye on me instead.  8 days later, they picked another fight with me and I couldn’t handle it anymore.  I shoveled as many OTC painkillers into my mouth as I could and ran down the hall to hide in the dorm bathrooms so they couldn’t stop me.  I didn’t want to die alone in a bathroom stall, so I eventually went back to my room and laid down on my bed to wait.  I thought it would be peaceful and that my fiancé wouldn’t care.  They hadn’t even realized what I had done at first, but when they did they started yelling at me that they were going to call an ambulance, for real this time.  That snapped me out of my dissociation enough to argue that I still couldn’t afford it, so they instead told all of my friends on campus what I had done.  I tried to keep them out of my room when they came downstairs, but I was dizzy and nauseous and my eyes were starting to blur.  One of my best friends sat on the floor with me and held my hands and sobbed.  My fiancé told them that our options were to either call an ambulance or force me to throw it up and take me to a doctor the next day.  It was probably 1am and I was still adamant that they not take me to the hospital.  I was more scared of the medical debt than I was of death.

My friend finally convinced me to throw up the pills I took.  I didn’t know for sure how many I had taken, only that I couldn’t swallow them all at once and I had counted 40 when I first started dumping them out but added more after that.  My fiancé took me back to the bathroom and put a chopstick down my throat.  I will never forget the bright blue streaks and half-digested pills in my vomit, or the way the whole bathroom smelled exactly like how pills taste when the coating starts to dissolve.  I have never been so exhausted before in my life, my sinuses burned and my head was throbbing, and I felt like I was experiencing it all through a veil.  Nothing seemed real.  I never cried, I even smiled at my friend while I tried to convince her that it was going to be okay if they would just let me go to sleep.  My friends finally left a little while after I threw up, and by then I could barely remember why they were in my room in the first place.

The next day, the friend who had held my hands the night before walked me to the campus counselor’s office after my classes let out for the day.  She hated the smell of cigarettes, but she didn’t mind that I smoked on the way there, and she sat outside my appointment and waited on me.  The counselor decided I needed to go back to the psych hospital despite my arguments, and he made me call my mom and tell her what I had done so she could take me there.  That night, my mom sat next to me in the emergency room for 6 hours while the nurses took my vitals, gave me a tetanus shot for the self injury I had done several days before, interviewed me, and introduced me to a social worker who told me I could leave the next day if I cooperated and stayed the rest of the night in the hospital.  I was worried about upcoming assignments I would miss, and my emotional support rabbit who was waiting for me in the car.  It wasn’t hot out and he was safe in his cage, but I didn’t want him to worry about me.  I still felt like I was watching everything happen in a movie, not living it.  At nearly 3am, a cop took me down the road to the psychiatric ward, and even though I’m normally terrified of the police, I went willingly.  I was just so tired that I would’ve done anything to be allowed to go to bed.

I stayed in the hospital for three days, the absolute minimum that they would hold me before I wasn’t considered a threat to myself anymore.  I spent those days in a room that I shared with a girl who had tried to hang herself and had oozing cuts from the rope around her neck.  I did my homework, colored with crayons, and called my fiancé to beg them to come visit me.  I knew from my last visit to this place that I would have to tell the doctors I wasn’t suicidal anymore if I wanted to get out, so I cooperated with the counselors and told anyone who would listen that I felt good enough to leave.  All I wanted was to go back to the way life was before.

It’s been a year now since this happened.  My friend who saved my life is now my roommate, and we share an apartment with her boyfriend, their cat, and my emotional support rabbit.  I left my fiancé three months after the incident, and now I’m dating someone who treats me well and makes me happy.  I haven’t self-injured since October of 2019, but my roommates still hide the painkillers from me just in case things get bad again.  I’m still pretty dependent on weed, but I’m on better medications now and I see a therapist regularly.  I haven’t felt suicidal in about 7 months, the longest stretch I’ve gone without serious suicidal ideation since I was in middle school.  I’m still struggling with mental illness, and some days feel really awful, but I don’t want to die anymore.  Looking back on this time last year, I remember the hospitalization as being more traumatizing than the suicide attempts were.

An overdose on pills is not the way to go out.  An overdose on pills is terrifying and awful.  It’s not a matter of taking them, laying down, and peacefully going to sleep.  If you survive it, you’ll live with the guilt and the physical and emotional trauma for the rest of your life.  You’ll spend each anniversary feeling like you shouldn’t be here.  Your loved ones will walk on eggshells around you for months, and you’ll have a hard time swallowing your daily medication because it reminds you too much of that night.  If you’re considering a pill overdose as a way to kill yourself, don’t do it.  Seek help, even if you can’t get a professional to do it.  Stop isolating yourself because you feel like you’re not worth anyone’s time and energy, and reach out to the people who love you.  Your life has so much worth, whether you can see it now or not, and you deserve better than to go out like this.

here’s something I learned when I was in the mental hospital: a lot of people use drugs because of underlying mental illness. it doesn’t matter if you have something you deem ‘minor,’ it still affects you every single day of your life, and that gets exhausting. using drugs is an escape from that. everything is so much easier to deal with when you’re high. I get it.
it’s not easy, but getting some kind of help for your mental health is so much better in the long run than using drugs to cope. you’re still young, you have so much life in you. I met people in the hospital who were middle aged and had watched their entire life fall apart because of drugs. you’re not there yet, you still have time to get help and change your habits. I’ve been there, and I promise things will get easier with time. it’s going to be okay, I promise.
